Re: Pilot Phase of the Framework for the U.S. Government's Engagement Related to Tech Platforms and
Mass Atrocities/Other Key Events
Overall

• What is your current regional and in-country representation for Burma and Bangladesh?

or mass atrocities (e.g. language, detection, staffing, scale of issues, lack appropriate local
contextual knowledge)?
• What are the relevant teams and internal stakeholders involved in the prevention of
violence around key events and atrocities? (in line with table in Annex 1 to concept note
re: Questions for Consideration in Engagement with Tech Platforms by Agencies, Bureaus)
What types of third party vendors or actors are involved in the monitoring and
enforcement of policies around prevention of violence and atrocities?
• Policy
From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): "Atrocity" should be defined, if loosely,
and potential perpetrators and victims identified. What best practices, industry standards
and/or evidentiary tests are there that social media companies can use to define atrocity,
perpetrator, and victim (especially in the context of complex inter-ethnic/inter-religious
• What policies or procedures do you have in place for addressing the use of your
products/services for the commission or incitement of mass atrocities or political violence
• What is the spectrum of policy responses your team considers? Are they
responsive to factors like proportionality or likelihood, etc?
• Where are these policies and procedures located? To what extent are they public
• Do these policies and procedures differ depending on your product/service?
• What language are these policies and procedures provided in? (Relevant to
Burma and Bangladesh)
• What processes and policies do you have in place to ensure that online harms (abuse,
harassment, calls for violence, and related disinformation) does not translate to offline
• How do you deal with regional or localized contextual nuance in global
operations, and the issue of linguistic diversity and colloquial terms (e.g. hate
speech terms about specific ethnic group in specific dialect.)
• In enforcement of your policies re: key events and atrocity prevention, what is the time
frame within which your team can adapt to new languages and/or regions? Or behaviors
that are contributing to violence or atrocities?

Other (relevant internal questions and issues for USG - State and USAID - during Pilot)
• From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): Glad to see "operating structure" as the first
agenda item. There is some concern that this initiative may
communication channels/processes typically led by other offices at State. We've also already
seen that communication between the State desk and post has been inconsistent/unclear. We
would appreciate clear guidance on the recommendation reporting relationship/ feedback
channels, considering the complexity emerging from the fact that we essentially have 4 units "at
post" -State in Yangon,State at DSU, USAID in Yangon, and USAID at DSU.
• Note, operating structure in agenda refers to Annex with questions, and org structure of
Meta, not USG organization,so important that we clarify this during the pilot
• From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): Given the origins of this initiative, we want to
reiterate (as is reflected in recent reporting from post) that we don't anticipate elections in the
near term, and certainly none that the USG would recognize, so we want to ensure framing doesn't
center around elections.
• From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): Although it's still early days, do we have a sense
of the anticipated or sought outcome(s) from this initiative?
• In the concept note we articulated the following potential outcomes of engagement via
the Framework for USAID/State:
• Improved understanding of the methodology used by tech platforms to assess the
risk of violence and mass atrocities and what tech platforms are and are not doing
at a global level to prevent or mitigate atrocities or violence related to key events.
• Improved prevention and response to challenging issues such as: online
harassment and abuse (with a gender lens, noting highly gendered nature),
disinformation and misinformation in select foreign markets, transparency, and
accountability on global and country specific challenges, opportunities, and good
practices.
• Improved information sharing and awareness raising of potential risk for harm
related to key events and atrocity prevention with tech platforms.
Sensitive but Unclassified

• Strengthened ongoingtechnical level engagement with tech platforms by USG
stakeholders through framework level engagement.
• Strengthened approaches to USG foreign policy and development programming
on key events andatrocity prevention due to improved understanding and
appreciation of tech platforms policies, systems, and processes, especially at a
national and local level. Relatedly, will help to improve human rights due diligence
and reputationalriskmanagement for USG engagements(programmatic and
policy).
• Message Administration prioritization of preventing violence related to key events
and mass atrocities to private sector partners.
• Wouldbe good to refine and discuss in line with engagements with platforms.
• From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): Strong recommendation to name this initiative
something clear and succinct to make coordination and communication more straightforward
(we've been saying 'tech company engagement on atrocity prevention thing' which is a bit of a
mouthful!).
• From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): As Post continues to regularly liaise with social
media companies, how can the USG incentivize companies to modify their community standards
and fair use policies when it is in a U.S. foreign policy interest, absent FCC regulations or federal
statutes?
• From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): USAID/Burma is currently working on an
assessment to respond to Congressional staffer engagements re: atrocity prevention in Burma
(primarily focused on exploring the potential of support to early warning/early response
interventions), and also a currently unrelated effort, at staffer invitation, to propose language for
the upcoming FY 24 Section 7043(a) 'Burma specific' appropriation provision, which will provide
funding to implement the authorizations of the Burma Act.
•From Burma team (USAID and State Pol/Econ): Post would appreciateclarity on potentially
thorny constitutional questions that are going to be hard to answer without greater elaboration
by Congress in the Communications Act, Communications Decency Act, or other Congressional
statute that relates to what could be perceived as interference in free speech/expression
platforms. Absent law enforcement requests predicated on federal statutes, how can social media
companies balance privacy concerns with sharing user data with federal agencies, including State
and USAID? What level of aggregation of user data (or how feasible to remove personal
identifiers) to allow for trend analysis in the context of atrocity prevention and mitigation?

Commented [16]: Is this question internal to the USG
or for Meta? If it is for Meta then USAID/GC has
serious concerns about this question. What does
"modify their community standards and fair use policies
when it is in a U.S. foreign policy interest" mean? This
portion of the question potentially raises reputational
risk for the USG and could be used to fuel arguments
that the USG is censoring or controlling media or
provide fodder for comparison to PRC actions limiting
or controlling free and independent media.
If it is for Meta, this question implies that the purpose(s)
of this meeting is to pressure companies to change
their community standards and fair use policies. More
importantly, the last clause "absent FCC regulations or
federal statutes" implies that the USG is seeking to do
an end run around the typical regulatory processes.
On the basis of what statutory or regulatory authority
would State or USAID be asking this question given
that fair use and community standards do not typically
fall under USAID or State's legal authorities?
For example, some might draw a negative inference
from the fact that agencies that do not regulate this
space are posing this question as opposed to the FCC
conducting consultations on this issue or being
included in these conversations.
